extracted.intended_audience: historians and philosophers of science, and scientists interested in paradigm change and the history of scientific revolutions
extracted.subtask_description: Analyze how scientific crises arise and how scientists respond, detailing the characteristics of anomalies, crisis dynamics, modes of closure, extraordinary research behavior, and the emergence and acceptance of new paradigms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crisis as a necessary precondition for novel theories
rubrics_metrics.description: Crises are typically a necessary precondition for the emergence of novel theories; the breakdown of normal problem-solving and the proliferation of competing theories tends to occur within a decade or two before the enunciation of a new theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kuhn notes that except for unusual cases (e.g., Copernicus), breakdowns and theory proliferation occur shortly before new theories are proposed. Problems that precipitate crises are often long recognized and previously considered solved, which intensifies the sense of failure when they resist normal methods. Historical examples: Copernicus, seventeenth-century combustion theories, and criticisms of Newton.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anomalies by themselves do not falsify paradigms
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientists confronted by anomalies do not renounce the paradigm or treat anomalies as straightforward counterinstances; paradigm rejection only happens when an alternative candidate is available to take its place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision to reject a paradigm is never just a comparison of that theory with nature — it is simultaneously a decision to accept another. Historical evidence suggests rejection resembles replacement, not simple falsification. The judgment leading to rejection involves comparison of both paradigms with nature and with each other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defenders will use articulations and ad hoc modifications
rubrics_metrics.description: When faced with anomalies, defenders of a paradigm will generally devise many articulations, qualifications, and ad hoc adjustments to eliminate apparent conflict rather than abandon the paradigm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These ad hoc moves are common in the literature; anomalies can at best create or reinforce crisis but often cannot, by themselves, overthrow a philosophical or scientific theory because its defenders will modify it to accommodate counterinstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of a paradigm without substitution equals rejection of science
rubrics_metrics.description: To reject one paradigm without simultaneously substituting another is effectively to reject science itself; such a move reflects on the individual, not the paradigm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kuhn argues that once a paradigm is in place, research without any paradigm is impossible. A scientist who abandons a paradigm without offering an alternative will be viewed as the person 'who blames his tools' and may leave the discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research presupposes a paradigm; puzzles vs. counterinstances
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no research in the absence of a paradigm; puzzles that constitute normal science exist because paradigms never resolve all problems — many puzzles can be construed as counterinstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kuhn emphasizes that normal science assumes the validity of the paradigm while solving puzzles. Examples: Copernicus, Lavoisier, Einstein perceive as counterinstances what others saw as solvable puzzles under the old paradigm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions that make an anomaly evoke crisis
rubrics_metrics.description: An anomaly must generally be more than a mere discrepancy to evoke crisis; certain features make an anomaly particularly pressing and worthy of concentrated scrutiny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors include: (a) the anomaly calls into question explicit and fundamental generalizations of the paradigm (e.g., ether drag and Maxwell), (b) the anomaly blocks applications of particular practical importance (e.g., calendar/astrology in Copernicus' case), (c) evolution of normal science can change an anomaly's status (e.g., weight relations in chemistry), and (d) long persistence or accumulation of residual discrepancies. Multiple factors often combine to render an anomaly crisis-worthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crisis dynamics: blurring paradigm and proliferation of partial solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Crisis begins with the blurring of a paradigm and the loosening of the rules for normal research, producing many divergent articulations and partial (often ad hoc) solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As anomalies resist, more practitioners attend to the problem; initial attacks follow paradigm rules but later attempts modify the paradigm in divergent ways. The result is decreased agreement about what the paradigm entails; Kuhn cites reactions by Copernicus, Einstein, and Pauli as illustrative of the felt breakdown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes by which crises close (three closure outcomes)
rubrics_metrics.description: All crises close in one of three ways: (1) normal science ultimately resolves the problem; (2) the problem resists and is set aside for future generations; (3) a new candidate paradigm emerges and a dispute follows over its acceptance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kuhn describes these as: (1) successful extension/articulation of the old paradigm to solve the anomaly (example: Clairaut resolving lunar perigee), (2) labeling and shelving the problem until better tools exist, and (3) reconstruction via a new paradigm leading to a struggle for acceptance — the last being the focus of paradigm-shift study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradigm shift as reconstruction, not cumulative extension
rubrics_metrics.description: A transition from one paradigm to another is a reconstruction of the field from new fundamentals rather than a cumulative extension of the old paradigm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The shift changes elementary theoretical generalizations, methods, and applications; while there is significant overlap in solvable problems between old and new paradigms during transition, the modes of solution differ decisively. Kuhn uses metaphors such as 'picking up the other end of the stick' and the gestalt shift to illustrate these qualitative changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of extraordinary research during crisis
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientists in crisis often concentrate on isolating and structuring the anomaly, magnifying the breakdown, pushing the paradigm's rules to their limits, conducting exploratory experiments, and generating speculative theories that can be tried and discarded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This research may appear somewhat random — trying experiments 'just to see what will happen' — and involves both empirical probing and speculative theorizing. Historical examples: Kepler's work on Mars, Priestley's investigations of gases, attempts to detect the neutrino, and tests of parity non-conservation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of philosophical analysis and thought experiments in crisis
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophical analysis and thought experiments often accompany and assist extraordinary research by exposing hidden assumptions and isolating the root of crises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normal science tends to hold creative philosophy at arm's length, but in periods of crisis philosophical scrutiny can weaken the hold of tradition and suggest foundations for new paradigms. Thought experiments (e.g., in Galileo, Einstein, Bohr) can isolate issues with clarity unattainable in laboratory experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crisis often proliferates new discoveries
rubrics_metrics.description: Concentrated attention on trouble spots during crises frequently produces multiple new discoveries, some accidental, some predictive, and some previously misinterpreted phenomena re-evaluated as significant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include the identification of oxygen in pneumatic chemistry, numerous optical discoveries preceding the wave theory of light (polarization, Poisson spot, colors of thin plates), and multiple discoveries around the emergence of quantum mechanics. Crisis both loosens stereotypes and supplies incremental data for paradigm change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innovators of new paradigms are often young or new to the field
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who achieve fundamental inventions of new paradigms are almost always very young or newcomers to the field, being less committed to traditional practice and more able to conceive alternative sets of rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kuhn suggests that relative lack of commitment to existing rules makes these individuals more likely to see that old rules no longer define a playable game and to invent replacements; this is an observed pattern rather than a strict rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science pedagogy and acceptance by authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Science pedagogy tends to entangle theory with its exemplary applications in ways that encourage students to accept theories on the authority of teacher and text rather than by independent evaluation of evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kuhn argues that applications in textbooks are taught as part of learning the paradigm, not as evidence; if applications were presented as evidence, omission of alternative interpretations or unsolved problems would be seen as bias. This pedagogical effect helps reinforce a confirmation-theory view among students.
